story.headline: The weekend's fears never hit markets, so the focus moved to data. A stronger China lifted the Australian dollar, while protests in France weighed on the euro.

reads.policy: Most central banks are holding in October and lining up for December, so the story is who raises rates first. The Bank of England and Bank of Japan look closest to hiking, which tends to pull money toward the pound and yen; the Fed, ECB and Bank of Canada are waiting on data.
reads.growth: China grew a little faster than expected, mostly because shoppers spent more, which is good news for countries that sell to China, like Australia. Elsewhere growth is steady but uneven, so this week inflation matters more for currencies than growth does.
reads.inflation: Prices are still rising too fast almost everywhere: US inflation came in hot three times last week and Europe's is at a three-year high, with expensive oil feeding it. That keeps central banks under pressure to hold rates high or raise them, and this week's UK, New Zealand and Japan readings decide how much.
reads.risk: The weekend's big fears, a Middle East flare-up or a surprise Iran deal, didn't happen, so markets stayed calm and the safe-haven currencies (yen, franc, dollar) got no extra lift. The stress point moved to France, where violent protests are weighing on the euro.
reads.tot: Oil is still expensive, around $100 a barrel or more, because shipping in the Gulf and Russian supply are both at risk. That helps oil exporters like Canada and hurts importers like Japan and the eurozone, and New Zealand's widening trade gap is a small drag on its dollar.
reads.positioning: Speculators aren't heavily leaned in most currencies, so there's little risk of a sudden rush for the exits. The exception is the Australian dollar: hedge funds already hold a lot of bets that it rises, so if the news turns it has the most room to fall.
reads.fiscal: Government finances are a slow-burning worry: the US deficit is the biggest in five years, and France's budget fight is making investors demand more to hold its debt. France is the one to watch this week, with a budget vote Tuesday and Moody's rating review Friday that can move the euro.

fed.summary: The Fed is expected to hold in October, then decide on a hike in December. Recent inflation has run hot, which keeps the dollar supported while markets wait.
fed.priced: October: hold expected; December: hike likely.
fed.why: Inflation is running hot and the government is borrowing heavily. That keeps long-term yields high and money flowing into the dollar.
fed.watch: The Fed is in its quiet period before the October 28 decision, so no Fed speakers. The real debate is whether December brings a hike.

boc.summary: A weak jobs report and a cautious business survey make an October hike unlikely, so the Bank of Canada looks set to hold on October 28. Today's inflation figure is the one thing that could change that.
boc.priced: October hike: about 1 in 4; December: likely.
boc.why: Canada lost jobs last month and unemployment rose, so markets pulled back on an October hike. Oil near $100 keeps inflation worries alive.
boc.watch: Today's inflation report. A hotter number brings the hike back; a cooler one makes a hold more likely.

rbnz.summary: The RBNZ is split between hiking and holding on October 28. Business activity is strong but trade and food prices are soft, so Wednesday's inflation figure will decide it.
rbnz.priced: October 28: close call between hike and hold.
rbnz.why: Business activity is the strongest in years, which points to a hike. A weaker trade balance and flat food prices point to waiting.
rbnz.watch: New Zealand's inflation figure on Wednesday decides it. The governor has said the next move is most likely up.

ecb.summary: The ECB is expected to hold in October and is leaning toward a hike in December, because inflation is at a three-year high. France's budget trouble is the main thing weighing on the euro.
ecb.priced: October: hold expected; December: hike likely.
ecb.why: Inflation hit a three-year high, driven by energy. Nearly every economist expects a hold in October, so the real debate is December.
ecb.watch: France. Protests and budget trouble are weighing on the euro, with a budget vote on Tuesday and a credit rating review on Friday. Lagarde speaks on Wednesday.

boj.summary: The BoJ keeps signalling that more rate hikes are coming, probably in December rather than October. Higher Japanese rates would narrow the gap with the US and support the yen.
boj.priced: October hike: about 1 in 4; December: likely.
boj.why: The governor said underlying inflation is close to the 2% goal, which firms up a December hike. October is still unlikely.
boj.watch: Japan's national inflation report on Friday. Also the yen near 160 per dollar, a level where Japan has stepped in before.

rba.summary: The RBA's tone has turned more hawkish, hinting rates may not be high enough yet. A hike in November is possible but not expected, and next week's inflation number is the key test.
rba.priced: November hike: about 1 in 3; December: a coin flip.
rba.why: The governor said rates may not be high enough yet and that the neutral level may be rising. Inflation is stuck near 3.6% while the job market loosens.
rba.watch: Australia's quarterly inflation report on October 28. It is the key test for a November hike.

boe.summary: The Bank of England is almost certain to raise rates on November 5, and the debate is already about December. This week's UK jobs and inflation data will shape how far it goes.
boe.why: A hike on November 5 is almost fully expected. The open question is whether the Bank keeps going in December.
boe.watch: UK jobs data on Tuesday, then inflation (expected to rise) and a Bailey speech on Wednesday. The UK budget follows on October 28.

snb.summary: The SNB is holding rates at zero and could even cut in December, because Swiss inflation is very low. The franc moves more on global fear than on Swiss news right now.
snb.priced: Holding at 0%; a December cut is possible.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is very soft, so the bank is on hold at zero with a December cut possible. The franc moves more on global fear than on Swiss news.
snb.watch: Thursday's write-up of the SNB's last meeting. Any rise in global fear would lift the franc regardless.
